opening_message:
Ticket 1: Ashley Roberts (employee ID E016) requests write access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E016.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Ashley Roberts (E016) is a full-time Analyst. Requested write access to Payroll. Full-time employees can have up to write, and admin requires owning the role; Analyst does not own Payroll. Requested level (write) is allowed, so recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E016 is a contractor with basic security training (note says Analyst). Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training; never admin. Basic training means max is read. Requested write is above max, so recommend read.
reason: The two notes conflict on a key fact: the HR-side note says E016 is full_time (recommending write), while the Security note says its database shows E016 is a contractor with basic security training, making the maximum access read (contractors need advanced training for write, and never admin). Given the conflicting employment records, I err on the side of the more restrictive verified status. As a contractor with basic training, the maximum allowed for Payroll is read, and the requested write is above that maximum, so I grant read.

If contractor with basic training: max is read → grant read.
